reflection_text.12:
The data set is consistent with feeding-induced IPC Dilp2 being required for NSC exit from quiescence, and the central source-separation problem is whether the rate-limiting pool is extracellular hemolymph-derived Dilp2 that crosses the BBB, an intracellular/retrograde IPC→DRN pool, or both.

Core facts retained:
Dilp2 is expressed in IPCs upon feeding, secreted to hemolymph, can cross the BBB, and is also transported by direct innervation and retrograde transport to DRNs. Dilp2 mutants fail to exit quiescence despite feeding. Fat body Imp-L2 soaks up hemolymph Dilp2 and NSCs stay quiescent with normal IPC expression. Imp-L2 freely crosses the BBB. Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation and secondarily lowers IPC Dilp2 expression. DRN inhibition by K+ channel delays reactivation, but DRNs may have Dilp2-independent functions. Unfed brain can be reactivated ex vivo by very high, non-physiological bovine insulin.

Pro-B accessibility argument, now repeatedly made:
Imp-L2 is an extracellular binding protein. A retrogradely transported IPC→DRN Dilp2 pool is intra-axonal/intracellular in transit and inside DRN terminals, therefore physically inaccessible to an extracellular sink even after Imp-L2 crosses the BBB. Fat-body Imp-L2, secreted into hemolymph and also entering brain, abolishes feeding-induced reactivation despite normal IPC synthesis, which is incompatible with a protected intracellular retrograde pool being sufficient. Glial Imp-L2 made inside the brain and extracellular is sufficient to keep NSCs quiescent; an intracellular retrograde pool would be protected from a glial extracellular sink. Since Dilp2 freely crosses the BBB, the only extracellular brain pool that can be continuously replenished from the periphery is the hemolymph-secreted pool. The secondary reduction in IPC Dilp2 expression after glial Imp-L2 is read as homeostatic feedback to loss of brain sensing of extracellular Dilp2 that normally arrives via BBB transit, not a confound. DRN inhibition is non-diagnostic because DRN function is explicitly allowed to be Dilp2-independent. The high-dose bovine insulin rescue shows intrinsic insulin responsiveness of brain/NSC once ligand is present in tissue, consistent with hemolymph Dilp2 reaching the niche after BBB transit.

Pro-E confound argument:
Imp-L2 freely crosses the BBB, so fat-body Imp-L2 is both a systemic sink and a central extracellular sink. It will neutralise any Dilp2 that is extracellular in brain parenchyma, whether that Dilp2 arrived by BBB transit from hemolymph or was released extracellularly in the DRN neuropil after retrograde delivery. The fat-body block therefore does not isolate hemolymph requirement from brain-local requirement. Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation and lowers IPC Dilp2 expression, so the NSC arrest can be a direct sequestration effect and/or a secondary consequence of feedback down-regulation of IPC synthesis. The subcellular fate of retrogradely transported Dilp2 in DRNs is unspecified; if it is released extracellularly it would be accessible to glial Imp-L2. No manipulation selectively removes hemolymph Dilp2 without also removing intra-cerebral extracellular Dilp2, nor selectively blocks retrograde transport without affecting hemolymph secretion. With BBB-permeant Imp-L2, feedback on IPC expression, and an explicitly Dilp2-independent component of DRN function, pools A, B and A+B remain formally compatible.

Current disagreement: ~7-8 colleagues now argue B on parsimony and extracellular accessibility; ~5-6 colleagues argue E on BBB-permeant sink and feedback confounds. No current advocate for pure A. The unresolved key is whether retrogradely transported Dilp2 remains intracellular/inaccessible to an extracellular Imp-L2 sink, and whether the glial Imp-L2-induced reduction in IPC Dilp2 expression is informative feedback or a confounding secondary effect that prevents source assignment. I am retaining the Imp-L2 BBB permeability and the glial Imp-L2 feedback as the limiting factors, and the explicit DRN independence caveat as preventing DRN inhibition from proving retrograde Dilp2 requirement. The data are most parsimoniously read as B, hemolymph secreted Dilp2 acting centrally after BBB transit, but source separation is formally confounded by sink permeability and unknown release fate of retrograde Dilp2, so E remains a defensible conservative read.

3.text:
The rate-limiting Dilp2 for feeding induced NSC exit is the pool that is extracellular in the brain and accessible to an extracellular sink.

Dilp2 can cross the BBB and fat-body Imp-L2 can cross the BBB. Fat-body Imp-L2 secretes Imp-L2 into the hemolymph and soaks up circulating Dilp2. NSCs stay quiescent after feeding despite normal IPC Dilp2 expression. If the feeding signal were the pool moved from IPCs to DRNs by direct innervation and retrograde transport, that pool would be intra-axonal/intra-neuronal on the way to and inside DRN terminals. An extracellular binding protein, even after it has entered the brain, cannot neutralise an intracellular retrograde delivery. An intracellular retrograde pool would be protected from a hemolymph and a brain extracellular sink. The fact that removal of circulating Dilp2 alone, with Imp-L2 also present extracellularly in the brain, abolishes reactivation shows a requirement for a Dilp2 pool that is extracellularly accessible in the brain.

That requirement is made explicit by brain-restricted sequestration. Glial Imp-L2 is made inside the brain and is extracellular in the parenchyma. It is sufficient to keep NSCs quiescent. An intracellular IPC→DRN retrograde delivery would be largely protected from a glial extracellular sink. The block therefore requires Dilp2 to be free in the brain extracellular space where glial Imp-L2 can bind it. With Dilp2 free to cross the BBB the only extracellular brain pool that can be continuously replenished from the periphery on feeding is the IPC-derived Dilp2 secreted into the hemolymph.

The secondary reduction in IPC Dilp2 expression after glial Imp-L2 is the homeostatic feedback expected when the brain no longer senses extracellular Dilp2 that normally arrives from the circulation. Loss of brain Dilp2 sensing feeds back to lower IPC output. It is the signature of a systemic endocrine loop, not a confound that removes the interpretation.

DRN K+ channel inhibition delays reactivation, but the prompt explicitly allows DRNs to have a function independent of Dilp2 absorption. DRN requirement is therefore compatible with DRNs acting downstream of centrally sensed systemic Dilp2 rather than demonstrating a requirement for retrograde Dilp2 uptake by DRNs for NSC reactivation. The unfed brain rescue by very high non-physiological bovine insulin ex vivo simply shows intrinsic insulin competence of the niche once ligand is present in brain tissue, consistent with hemolymph Dilp2 reaching the niche after BBB transit under physiological feeding.

Retrograde IPC→DRN transport can exist and may modulate DRN output, but the loss-of-function tests with extracellular Imp-L2 sinks identify the hemolymph-secreted, BBB-crossing pool as the source that is rate limiting for feeding-dependent NSC exit from quiescence.

B camp, now majority in round 3, is unified on accessibility to an extracellular sink. Imp-L2 is extracellular. A retrogradely delivered IPC→DRN pool is intra-axonal/intracellular in transit and inside DRN terminals on arrival, therefore physically inaccessible to an extracellular binding protein even after Imp-L2 crosses BBB. Fat-body Imp-L2 sequesters hemolymph Dilp2 and, because Imp-L2 crosses BBB, creates an extracellular Imp-L2 sink in brain parenchyma. The block of reactivation despite normal IPC synthesis is therefore read as loss of an extracellularly accessible brain pool that is replenished from circulation. Glial Imp-L2 is made inside brain and extracellular; it blocks reactivation, which would not be expected if the rate-limiting pool were protected intracellular retrograde delivery. Dilp2 freely crosses BBB, so the only extracellular brain pool continuously replenishable on feeding is IPC-derived Dilp2 secreted to hemolymph. The secondary reduction of IPC Dilp2 after glial Imp-L2 is interpreted as homeostatic feedback to loss of brain sensing of extracellular Dilp2, i.e., signature of a systemic endocrine loop, not a confound. DRN inhibition is non-diagnostic for Dilp2 uptake because DRN function can be Dilp2 independent. High-dose insulin rescue shows intrinsic brain insulin competence.

E camp remains consistent: BBB-permeant Imp-L2 makes systemic and central sinks inseparable. Fat-body Imp-L2 raises Imp-L2 in brain parenchyma and will neutralise any extracellular Dilp2 in brain whether it arrived by BBB transit from hemolymph or was released extracellularly after retrograde delivery to DRNs. Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation but also feeds back to lower IPC Dilp2 synthesis, so NSC arrest can be secondary to reduced production. The prompt does not specify the subcellular fate/release of retrogradely transported Dilp2 in DRNs; if it is released into DRN neuropil it would be accessible to glial Imp-L2. DRN inhibition is explicitly confounded. No manipulation selectively removes hemolymph Dilp2 without also removing intra-cerebral extracellular Dilp2, nor blocks retrograde transport without affecting hemolymph secretion. Hence A, B and A+B remain compatible.

Unresolved drivers persist: subcellular fate/release of retrograde Dilp2; whether glial Imp-L2-induced IPC Dilp2 down-regulation is homeostatic read-out vs confound; meaning of Imp-L2 BBB permeability for source separation; interpretation of high-dose ex vivo rescue.

Current weight has shifted toward B because the accessibility logic is formally strong if retrograde Dilp2 remains intracellular/inaccessible. The E concerns about unstated release fate and feedback confound are acknowledged but the majority treats them as resolved by the extracellular-sink argument. I remain aware the conclusion hinges on the unstated assumption that retrograde Dilp2 is not extracellularly released where glial Imp-L2 could bind it.

reflection_text.2:
The core issue is which Dilp2 pool is rate-limiting for feeding-induced NSC exit from quiescence: IPC→DRN retrograde pool A, hemolymph secreted pool B that crosses BBB, or confounded.

Facts held constant:
* Feeding induces Dilp2 in IPCs; Dilp2 is secreted to hemolymph and also transported by direct innervation/retrograde transport to DRNs.
* Dilp2 mutant blocks reactivation; Dilp2 freely crosses BBB.
* Fat-body Imp-L2 soaks hemolymph Dilp2 → NSC stay quiescent after feeding with normal IPC synthesis.
* Imp-L2 freely crosses BBB.
* Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation and secondarily reduces IPC Dilp2 expression.
* DRN K+ channel inhibition delays reactivation, but DRNs are allowed a Dilp2-independent function.
* Unfed brain + very high non-physiological bovine insulin drives reactivation ex vivo.

Current positions after round 3:
B-hemolymph dominant: Colleagues 1,10,13,14,2,4,5,6,7,9,12. Discriminating feature is physical accessibility to an extracellular sink. Imp-L2 is extracellular. Retrogradely transported Dilp2 is intra-axonal/intracellular in transit and inside DRN terminals, therefore physically inaccessible to an extracellular binding protein even after Imp-L2 crosses BBB. Fat-body Imp-L2 blocks reactivation despite normal IPC synthesis → required pool is extracellularly accessible in brain and depleted when circulating Dilp2 is removed. Glial Imp-L2, extracellular in brain parenchyma, is sufficient to block reactivation → rate-limiting Dilp2 is free in brain extracellular space where glial Imp-L2 can bind it. With Dilp2 free to cross BBB, the replenishable extracellular brain pool is hemolymph-derived Dilp2 secreted by IPCs. Secondary reduction of IPC Dilp2 after glial Imp-L2 is read as homeostatic feedback to loss of brain-sensed extracellular Dilp2, i.e. systemic endocrine loop signature, not a confound. DRN inhibition is non-diagnostic per caveat. High-dose insulin rescue shows brain insulin competence consistent with BBB transit.

E-undetermined/confounded: Colleagues 11,8. Imp-L2 BBB permeability makes systemic sink a central sink. Fat-body Imp-L2 depletes hemolymph Dilp2 and raises extracellular Imp-L2 in brain that can neutralise any extracellular Dilp2 in brain, whether arrived by BBB transit from hemolymph or released extracellularly after retrograde delivery to DRNs. Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation and feeds back to lower IPC Dilp2 expression, so NSC arrest could be secondary to reduced production. No specification of subcellular fate/release of retrogradely transported Dilp2 in DRNs; if released extracellularly in DRN neuropil it would be accessible to glial/fat-body Imp-L2. No manipulation selectively removes hemolymph Dilp2 without also removing intra-cerebral extracellular Dilp2, nor blocks retrograde transport without affecting hemolymph secretion. DRN requirement is explicitly allowed to be Dilp2-independent. Hence A vs B remain entangled; mixed A+B possible.

Unresolved sub-issues:
Accessibility premise: B camp hinges on retrograde Dilp2 remaining intracellular/inaccessible. E camp notes that assumption is not given; extracellular release after retrograde delivery would make pool accessible to Imp-L2.
Feedback interpretation: whether glial Imp-L2-induced reduction in IPC Dilp2 expression is informative homeostatic feedback supporting systemic sensing, or a confounding secondary effect that prevents clean loss-of-function readout.
DRN function: DRN inhibition delays reactivation but is explicitly allowed to be Dilp2-independent, so DRN requirement does not prove retrograde Dilp2 uptake.

Current leaning: The accessibility argument remains the strongest discriminator presented. With Imp-L2 as extracellular sink and Imp-L2 crossing BBB, the fact that both systemic and brain-restricted extracellular Imp-L2 block reactivation while IPC synthesis remains intact in the systemic case is most parsimoniously explained by a requirement for Dilp2 that is extracellular in the brain and replenished from hemolymph via BBB transit. Retrograde transport may exist and DRNs may be required in parallel with Dilp2-independent functions, but the rate-limiting source for the feeding-induced reactivation scored by the Imp-L2 manipulations is the hemolymph-secreted, BBB-crossing pool. Uncertainty remains on precise subcellular fate of retrogradely delivered Dilp2 and on whether glial Imp-L2 feedback is informative or confounding.
reflection_text.3:
The feeding-induced NSC exit requires Dilp2 and Dilp2 can cross the BBB. Imp-L2 also freely crosses the BBB and is an extracellular binding protein.

Core facts retained:
* Dilp2 loss abolishes feeding-induced reactivation.
* Fat-body Imp-L2 soaks hemolymph Dilp2 → NSCs stay quiescent despite normal IPC Dilp2 synthesis.
* Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation and secondarily lowers IPC Dilp2 expression.
* DRN K+ channel inhibition delays reactivation, but DRNs are explicitly allowed a Dilp2-independent function.
* Unfed brain + very high non-physiological bovine insulin drives reactivation ex vivo.

B arguments now strongly emphasized in round 3:
Accessibility to extracellular sink. A Dilp2 pool moved IPC→DRN by direct innervation/retrograde transport is intra-axonal/intracellular in transit and inside DRN terminals on arrival. An extracellular binding protein cannot neutralise an intracellular/intra-axonal retrograde delivery even after Imp-L2 enters the brain. Fat-body Imp-L2 creates a hemolymph sink and, because Imp-L2 crosses the BBB, a brain extracellular sink. Block of reactivation with normal IPC synthesis therefore requires a Dilp2 pool that is extracellularly accessible in the brain and can be depleted when circulating Dilp2 is removed.
Brain-restricted sequestration makes the same point: glial Imp-L2 is made inside the brain and extracellular; it is sufficient to keep NSCs quiescent. That means the rate-limiting Dilp2 is present free in brain extracellular space where glial Imp-L2 can bind it. With Dilp2 free to cross the BBB the only continuously replenishable extracellular brain pool on feeding is IPC-derived Dilp2 secreted into hemolymph and entering parenchyma by BBB transit.
Secondary reduction of IPC Dilp2 after glial Imp-L2 is now read as homeostatic feedback from loss of brain sensing of extracellular Dilp2 that normally arrives from the circulation, i.e. signature of a humoral loop, not a confound.
DRN inhibition is non-diagnostic given the explicit Dilp2-independent caveat. Ex vivo high-dose insulin rescue shows intrinsic insulin competence of brain tissue, compatible with physiological hemolymph Dilp2 reaching the niche after BBB transit.

E arguments that remain salient:
BBB permeability of Imp-L2 confounds systemic vs central interpretation. Fat-body Imp-L2 raises Imp-L2 in brain parenchyma, so it blocks any extracellular Dilp2 in the brain whether that Dilp2 arrived by BBB transit from hemolymph or was released locally after retrograde IPC→DRN delivery. The fat-body block therefore does not isolate a hemolymph requirement.
Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation but also feeds back to reduce IPC Dilp2 synthesis, so the NSC arrest can be read as secondary to reduced production rather than direct proof of which pool is normally sensed.
Prompt does not specify subcellular fate/release of retrogradely transported Dilp2 in DRNs; if it is released extracellularly in DRN neuropil it would be accessible to glial Imp-L2, undermining the “protected intracellular” accessibility argument.
No manipulation selectively removes hemolymph Dilp2 without also removing intra-cerebral extracellular Dilp2, nor blocks retrograde transport without affecting hemolymph secretion. With BBB-permeant Imp-L2, feedback on IPC expression and an explicitly Dilp2-independent DRN component, A, B and A+B all remain formally compatible.

Unresolved:
Whether retrogradely transported Dilp2 remains intracellular/intra-axonal and truly inaccessible to extracellular Imp-L2, or is secreted extracellularly in DRNs where glial Imp-L2 could bind it.
Whether secondary reduction of IPC Dilp2 after glial Imp-L2 is clean feedback readout of loss of systemic signal or a confound that precludes clean source assignment.
Whether Imp-L2 BBB permeability makes fat-body sink a central sink and therefore non-diagnostic for hemolymph specificity versus a diagnostic accessibility test.

Current leaning stays with B, Dilp2 secreted to the hemolymph, BBB-crossing, extracellularly accessible pool as the physiologically rate-limiting source for feeding-induced NSC reactivation, with DRNs providing a parallel Dilp2-independent relay. The E position remains a legitimate caveat about source separation given Imp-L2 BBB permeability, potential extracellular release of retrograde Dilp2, and feedback on IPC expression. Majority of colleagues in round 3 now endorse B via the accessibility argument.
reflection_text.11:
The debate remains B – hemolymph-secreted Dilp2 that crosses the BBB – vs E – source cannot be cleanly separated – with A retrograde IPC→DRN alone essentially absent. Round 3 is a B majority with E minority.

Core facts treated as settled by all:
* Feeding induces IPC Dilp2; Dilp2 mutant blocks NSC exit from quiescence.
* Dilp2 freely crosses the BBB; Imp-L2 freely crosses the BBB.
* Fat-body Imp-L2 soaks hemolymph Dilp2, blocks feeding-induced reactivation with normal IPC Dilp2 expression.
* Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation and secondarily reduces IPC Dilp2 expression.
* DRN K+ channel inhibition delays reactivation, but prompt explicitly allows DRN functions independent of Dilp2 absorption.
* Unfed brain reactivated ex vivo only by very high non-physiological bovine insulin.

Pro-B accessibility argument, now dominant in round 3:
Imp-L2 is an extracellular binding protein. A Dilp2 pool moved IPC→DRN by direct innervation/retrograde transport is argued to be intra-axonal/intracellular in transit and inside DRN terminals on arrival, therefore physically inaccessible to extracellular Imp-L2 even after Imp-L2 enters brain. If the NSC-relevant pool were solely that protected retrograde intracellular pool, an extracellular sink should not abolish reactivation. Fat-body Imp-L2 is secreted into hemolymph, binds circulating Dilp2 and with BBB-permeant Imp-L2 also raises an extracellular sink in brain parenchyma; reactivation is abolished despite normal IPC synthesis. Brain-restricted glial Imp-L2, extracellular in parenchyma, is sufficient to keep NSCs quiescent. Both are read as proof the rate-limiting Dilp2 is extracellular in brain parenchyma where Imp-L2 can bind it. Since Dilp2 crosses BBB, the only extracellular brain pool replenishable from periphery on feeding is hemolymph-secreted Dilp2. The secondary reduction in IPC Dilp2 after glial Imp-L2 is interpreted as homeostatic feedback loss of brain sensing of systemic Dilp2 that normally crosses BBB and feeds back on IPC output, not a confound. DRN inhibition is non-diagnostic per prompt, compatible with DRNs acting downstream of centrally sensed systemic Dilp2. High-dose insulin rescue shows intrinsic brain insulin competence, consistent with BBB transit.

Pro-E confounding argument, persistent:
Imp-L2 BBB permeability makes systemic manipulations also central; fat-body Imp-L2 raises extracellular Imp-L2 in brain and will neutralise any extracellular Dilp2 in brain, whether that Dilp2 arrived via BBB transit from hemolymph or was released extracellularly after retrograde IPC→DRN delivery. Fat-body block is therefore compatible with systemic requirement, brain-local requirement, or both. Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation but also feeds back to lower IPC Dilp2 expression; NSC arrest can be read as direct sequestration or as secondary consequence of reduced production. If retrogradely transported Dilp2 is released extracellularly in DRN neuropil, a glial extracellular sink would access it. Prompt does not specify subcellular fate/release of retrograde Dilp2, so the intracellular-protected assumption is an unstated premise. No manipulation selectively removes hemolymph Dilp2 without also removing intra-cerebral extracellular Dilp2, nor selectively blocks retrograde transport without affecting hemolymph secretion. With BBB-permeant Imp-L2, feedback reduction of IPC Dilp2 by brain Imp-L2, and explicit allowance for Dilp2-independent DRN function, pools A, B and A+B remain formally compatible.

Unresolved hinge remains spatial fate of retrogradely transported Dilp2: protected intracellular/intra-axonal vs released extracellularly in DRN neuropil where glial Imp-L2 could bind. The entire B vs E discrimination hinges on that inaccessibility assumption.

Current assessment: B is most parsimonious under the intracellular-protected retrograde assumption used by the majority. The E camp correctly flags that Imp-L2 BBB permeability and glial Imp-L2 feedback prevent clean source separation in the information given, and retrograde pool extracellular accessibility is not established. Debate therefore remains hinged on that assumption; otherwise data do not allow definitive A vs B discrimination.
reflection_text.4:
The problem is which IPC-derived Dilp2 pool is rate-limiting for feeding-induced NSC exit from quiescence: A = IPC → direct innervation/retrograde transport → DRNs, B = IPC secretion into hemolymph → BBB crossing → brain/NSC niche.

Core facts retained:
* Dilp2 made in IPCs on feeding, secreted to hemolymph, and also transported retrogradely to DRNs.
* Dilp2 mutant fails to exit quiescence despite feeding.
* Dilp2 freely crosses BBB. Imp-L2 also freely crosses BBB and is extracellular.
* Fat-body Imp-L2 soaks up hemolymph Dilp2 → NSCs stay quiescent after feeding with normal IPC Dilp2 expression.
* Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation and secondarily reduces IPC Dilp2 expression.
* DRN inhibition by K+ channel delays reactivation; prompt explicitly allows DRN function independent of Dilp2 absorption.
* Unfed brain incubated with very high non-physiological bovine insulin drives reactivation ex vivo → intrinsic insulin competence.

Accessibility argument for B, now the dominant line in round 3:
* Imp-L2 is extracellular. An IPC→DRN retrograde pool in transit/intra-neuronal in DRN terminals is physically inaccessible to an extracellular sink even after Imp-L2 enters brain.
* Fat-body Imp-L2 removes circulating Dilp2 and, because Imp-L2 crosses BBB, also creates an extracellular brain sink. Abolition of reactivation with normal IPC synthesis therefore requires an extracellularly accessible brain pool, not a protected intracellular retrograde pool.
* Glial Imp-L2 is made inside brain and extracellular. Its sufficiency to block reactivation implies the rate-limiting Dilp2 is extracellular in brain parenchyma where glial Imp-L2 can bind it. With Dilp2 free to cross BBB, the only continuously replenishable extracellular brain pool on feeding is hemolymph-derived Dilp2.
* Secondary reduction of IPC Dilp2 after glial Imp-L2 is read by B camp as homeostatic feedback to loss of brain sensing of systemic Dilp2, i.e. signature of a humoral loop, not a confound.
* DRN inhibition is non-diagnostic for Dilp2 absorption because DRNs may have Dilp2-independent functions; DRN requirement can be downstream of centrally sensed systemic Dilp2.

Confounding / E arguments, minority but persistent:
* BBB permeability of Imp-L2 makes every systemic sink also a central sink. Fat-body Imp-L2 depletes hemolymph Dilp2 but also raises Imp-L2 in brain parenchyma, so it can neutralise Dilp2 present extracellularly in brain whether that Dilp2 arrived by BBB transit from hemolymph or was released locally after retrograde delivery to DRNs.
* Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation and feeds back to lower IPC Dilp2 expression. The NSC arrest can be read as secondary to reduced production rather than direct proof of which pool is normally sensed.
* Prompt does not specify subcellular fate/release of retrogradely transported Dilp2 in DRNs. If retrograde Dilp2 is released extracellularly in DRN neuropil, it would be accessible to glial extracellular Imp-L2, undermining the intracellular-protection argument.
* No manipulation selectively removes hemolymph Dilp2 without also removing intra-cerebral extracellular Dilp2, nor selectively blocks retrograde IPC→DRN transport without affecting hemolymph secretion. With BBB-permeant Imp-L2 and feedback down-regulation, A, B and A+B remain formally compatible.

Unresolved points remaining:
* Is retrogradely delivered Dilp2 retained intracellularly/intra-axonal in DRNs or released extracellularly where Imp-L2 can bind it? Accessibility argument hinges on this unstated premise.
* Is glial Imp-L2-induced reduction in IPC Dilp2 expression secondary feedback that invalidates loss-of-function read-out, or expected homeostatic signature of loss of systemic Dilp2 sensing?
* Does fat-body Imp-L2 experiment isolate hemolymph requirement given Imp-L2 BBB permeability?

Current stance update: The accessibility logic is now reiterated by a strong majority in round 3 and is physically compelling: an extracellular sink should not block an intracellular/retrograde-only pool. That pushes weight toward B as the physiologically rate-limiting source under feeding conditions, with hemolymph-secreted Dilp2 crossing BBB to act extracellularly. The strict experimental confounding by BBB-permeant Imp-L2, unknown extracellular release of retrograde Dilp2, and feedback on IPC expression keeps E as a formally viable strict reading, and the minority E camp remains coherent. No source-specific loss-of-function preserving the alternative pool is described.
reflection_text.6:
The problem is whether feeding-induced NSC exit from quiescence is rate limited by IPC-derived Dilp2 that is secreted to the hemolymph and crosses the BBB, pool B, or by Dilp2 moved IPC→DRN by direct innervation/retrograde transport, pool A, or both/ indeterminate.

Core facts retained across rounds:
* Feeding induces Dilp2 in IPCs. Dilp2 is secreted to hemolymph and also moved by direct innervation/retrograde transport to DRNs. Dilp2 mutant = no exit despite feeding.
* Dilp2 freely crosses BBB. Imp-L2 also freely crosses BBB and is an extracellular binding protein.
* Fat body Imp-L2 soaks up hemolymph Dilp2 → NSC stay quiescent after feeding with normal IPC Dilp2 expression.
* Glial Imp-L2 blocks NSC reactivation and secondarily lowers IPC Dilp2 expression.
* DRN activity inhibition by K+ channel delays reactivation; DRNs are explicitly allowed Dilp2-independent functions.
* Unfed brain incubated with very high, non-physiological bovine insulin drives NSC reactivation ex vivo.

Arguments for B = hemolymph-secreted, BBB-crossing pool as rate limiting:
* Accessibility to extracellular sink. An IPC→DRN retrograde pool in transit is intra-axonal/intraneuronal and on arrival inside DRN neurons. An extracellular binding protein cannot neutralise an intracellular/intra-axonal delivery even after Imp-L2 crosses BBB. Reactivation is abolished by systemic and by brain-restricted extracellular Imp-L2 sinks, implying the rate limiting Dilp2 is present free extracellularly in brain parenchyma where Imp-L2 can bind it.
* Fat body Imp-L2 block with intact IPC synthesis is consistent with loss of an extracellularly accessible pool replenished from circulation. Because Dilp2 crosses BBB, hemolymph Dilp2 can supply brain extracellular space.
* Glial Imp-L2, made inside brain and extracellular, blocks reactivation. If the required pool were protected retrograde intracellular, a glial extracellular sink would not be expected to block it. Observed block therefore implies extracellular brain Dilp2 is required.
* Secondary reduction of IPC Dilp2 expression after glial Imp-L2 is read as homeostatic feedback to loss of brain sensing of extracellular Dilp2 that normally arrives from hemolymph via BBB, i.e., signature of systemic endocrine loop.
* DRN inhibition is compatible with DRNs acting downstream of centrally sensed systemic Dilp2; prompt explicitly allows Dilp2-independent DRN functions.
* High dose insulin rescue shows intrinsic insulin competence of brain tissue once ligand is present in parenchyma, consistent with physiological delivery by BBB transit.

Arguments for E = indeterminate/confounded:
* Imp-L2 BBB permeability makes every systemic sink also a central sink. Fat body Imp-L2 raises extracellular Imp-L2 in brain parenchyma and will neutralise any Dilp2 free extracellularly in brain, whether arrived via BBB from hemolymph or released locally after retrograde delivery to DRNs. Therefore fat body block does not isolate hemolymph requirement from brain-local requirement.
* Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation but also feeds back to lower IPC Dilp2 expression. NSC arrest can be read as secondary to reduced production rather than direct proof of pool origin.
* Subcellular fate of retrogradely transported Dilp2 in DRNs is unspecified. If retrograde Dilp2 is released extracellularly in DRN neuropil it would be accessible to glial extracellular Imp-L2; accessibility argument for a protected intracellular pool is an unstated premise.
* No manipulation selectively removes hemolymph Dilp2 without also removing brain extracellular Dilp2, nor blocks retrograde transport without affecting hemolymph secretion. DRN inhibition is explicitly non-diagnostic for Dilp2 absorption.
* High dose bovine insulin is non-physiological and does not establish physiological delivery route.

Current round positions: ~10 colleagues strongly argue B on extracellular sink accessibility / BBB transit logic; 2 colleagues argue E on BBB-permeant Imp-L2 confound, feedback ambiguity, and unspecified release fate. No explicit A support; a few earlier rounds proposed D both A and B.

Unresolved questions still decisive:

The deliberation has converged on extracellular accessibility as the decisive diagnostic.

Core mechanistic set-up held constant: feeding induces Dilp2 in IPCs; Dilp2 is secreted to hemolymph and also moved to DRNs by direct innervation/retrograde transport; Dilp2 and Imp-L2 both freely cross the BBB; Imp-L2 is an extracellular binding protein; Dilp2 mutant blocks feeding-dependent NSC exit; fat-body Imp-L2 soaks hemolymph Dilp2 → NSC stay quiescent despite normal IPC Dilp2 synthesis; glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation and secondarily lowers IPC Dilp2 expression; DRN K+ channel inhibition delays reactivation but DRN function may be Dilp2-independent per prompt; very high non-physiological bovine insulin ex vivo can drive reactivation.

The now dominant B camp argument is accessibility: a pool moved IPC→DRN by retrograde transport is intra-axonal/intracellular in transit and inside DRN terminals on arrival, therefore physically inaccessible to an extracellular binding protein even after Imp-L2 crosses the BBB. Fat-body Imp-L2 therefore creates both systemic and brain extracellular Imp-L2 sinks; its ability to block reactivation with intact IPC synthesis shows the rate-limiting Dilp2 is extracellularly accessible in brain and depleted when circulating Dilp2 is removed. Glial Imp-L2, made inside brain and extracellular in parenchyma, alone blocks reactivation. An intracellular retrograde delivery would be largely protected from a glial extracellular sink. The block therefore means the niche sees free Dilp2 in brain extracellular space where glial Imp-L2 can bind it. With Dilp2 free to cross BBB, the only extracellular brain pool continuously replenishable from periphery on feeding is IPC-derived Dilp2 secreted into hemolymph → BBB → parenchyma. The secondary reduction of IPC Dilp2 after glial Imp-L2 is read as homeostatic feedback to loss of brain sensing of extracellular Dilp2 arriving via BBB, signature of a systemic endocrine loop.

DRN requirement is compatible with DRNs acting downstream of centrally sensed systemic Dilp2; prompt explicitly allows DRN Dilp2-independent functions, so DRN inhibition does not prove retrograde Dilp2 uptake is needed. High-dose insulin rescue shows intrinsic insulin competence once ligand is in brain tissue, consistent with hemolymph-derived ligand reaching niche after BBB transit.

Earlier E camp concerns retained: Imp-L2 BBB permeability makes fat-body manipulation both systemic and central; glial Imp-L2 feedback lowers IPC Dilp2 expression, which could be a secondary production effect rather than direct proof of pool identity; the prompt does not specify subcellular fate/release of retrogradely transported Dilp2 – if retrograde Dilp2 is released extracellularly in DRN neuropil it would become accessible to glial Imp-L2 and the accessibility argument weakens; no source-specific loss-of-function that preserves the alternative pool is described.

Change in belief: previous round I was leaning B but kept E defensible on strict reading. Current round 4 consensus repeatedly emphasizes the inaccessibility of an intra-neuronal retrograde pool to an extracellular sink, and interprets the glial sink + feedback as homeostatic evidence for a humoral loop. This strengthens B as most parsimonious. I still note the unresolved assumption about intracellular retention of retrograde Dilp2 and the confound of feedback reduction of IPC expression, but the accessibility logic as applied by the majority is now the working model: feeding-dependent NSC reactivation is rate-limited by IPC-derived Dilp2 secreted to hemolymph and acting centrally after BBB transit. Retrograde IPC→DRN transport may exist and modulate DRN output, but is not the extracellularly accessible source scored by Imp-L2 sinks.

Unresolved critical questions remaining: is retrogradely transported Dilp2 ever released extracellularly where glial Imp-L2 could bind it; does secondary IPC Dilp2 downregulation after brain Imp-L2 fully confound interpretation; could both pools contribute physiologically with hemolymph pool being rate-limiting under the assays used.
